name: Embedded Figures — Spotting and Counting Hidden Shapes
whatIsIt: Embedded figure questions hide a simple shape inside a more complex, overlapping one, and ask you to find it — or to count exactly how many shapes of a certain kind (like triangles) are hiding inside a figure once you include the ones formed by COMBINING smaller regions together.
whyNeeded: This trains systematic visual scanning instead of guessing: counting every small region first, then every possible combination of adjacent regions, so you never miss a hidden or combined shape.
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of SSC, banking, and railway exams
Reading complex technical diagrams and blueprints
Careful, exhaustive visual counting in general

vocabulary.meaning: A simple shape hidden inside a more complex figure, formed by some of its lines.
One of the smallest separate areas a complex figure is divided into by its lines.
A larger shape formed by joining two or more adjacent regions together.

story.title: The Diagonal Square
story.text: Meera draws a square and both its diagonals, crossing in the middle. 'How many triangles can you find?' she asks. Kabir counts the 4 small triangles made by the crossing diagonals — 1, 2, 3, 4. 'Good start,' says Meera, 'but look again — each HALF of the square, cut by just one diagonal, is ALSO a triangle, made of two small ones joined together.' Kabir finds 4 more of those. '4 small plus 4 combined — 8 triangles total!' he says, surprised he'd missed half of them at first.
story.extractedProblem: A square has both its diagonals drawn, crossing at the center. How many triangles are there in total?
story.answerInStory: 8 triangles — 4 small ones from the crossing diagonals, plus 4 larger ones formed by combining two small triangles across each diagonal.

visual.caption: Systematically scan a complex figure region by region — a 5-pointed star, for example, is built from 5 overlapping triangles, each one a hidden embedded shape.

teachingGallery.title: Small regions first, then combinations
teachingGallery.note: Never count only the smallest visible regions — always ALSO check every way two or more adjacent regions can combine into a bigger version of the target shape.

examples.caption: A square split by both diagonals gives 4 small triangles — but combining adjacent pairs across each diagonal gives 4 MORE (larger) triangles, for 8 total.

standardMethod.summary: First count every smallest separate region that matches the target shape. Then systematically check every possible combination of 2, 3, or more ADJACENT regions to see if that combination also forms the target shape. Add both counts together for the total.
steps: Identify the target shape you're counting or searching for (e.g. triangles).
Count every smallest individual region matching that shape first.
Check every pair of adjacent regions — does combining them form a larger version of the target shape too?
Check larger combinations (3+ regions) if the figure is complex enough to have them.
Add all matching counts together for the final total — never stop after just the smallest regions.

alternateMethods.name: Vertex-triangulation formula (for polygons split from one corner)
alternateMethods.whenToUse: A polygon with all diagonals drawn from a single vertex.
steps: Count the number of sides of the polygon (n).
The number of triangles formed is always n − 2, when all diagonals are drawn from just one vertex.
alternateMethods.example: A hexagon (6 sides) triangulated from one vertex gives 6 − 2 = 4 triangles.

workedExamples.problem: A square has both diagonals drawn, crossing at the center. How many triangles are there in total?
steps: Count the smallest regions: the two diagonals cross to form 4 small triangles.
Check combinations: each diagonal alone splits the square into 2 halves, and each half (made of 2 small triangles) is itself a bigger triangle — that's 4 more (2 halves per diagonal × 2 diagonals).

workedExamples.problem: A pentagon (5 sides) has all its diagonals drawn from just ONE vertex. How many triangles does this create?
steps: Use the vertex-triangulation formula: triangles = n − 2, where n is the number of sides.

trickPractice.trick: Count small regions first, THEN check every combination
trickPractice.intro: Missing the combined (larger) shapes is the single most common error — always check combinations after the small regions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping after counting only the smallest visible regions, missing the larger shapes formed by combining adjacent regions.
commonMistakes.fix: Always ask 'can I combine two or more adjacent regions into the target shape too?' after counting the smallest ones — this step is where most of the missed shapes hide.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting the same combined shape more than once by approaching it from different starting regions.
commonMistakes.fix: Track counted shapes systematically (e.g. by labeling regions 1, 2, 3... and listing exactly which region-numbers make up each shape you count) to avoid counting the same one twice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Misremembering or misapplying the n−2 vertex-triangulation formula, such as using it for diagonals drawn from multiple different vertices (where it doesn't apply).
commonMistakes.fix: The n−2 formula only works when ALL diagonals come from a single vertex. If diagonals come from multiple vertices or cross each other, count small regions and combinations by hand instead.

revisionCard.summary: Count every smallest individual region matching the target shape first, then systematically check every combination of adjacent regions for larger matching shapes — add both counts together. For polygons with all diagonals from a single vertex, use the shortcut n − 2 (sides minus 2) to find the triangle count directly.

gameMission.title: Hidden Shapes in the Canopy
gameMission.brief: Search the jungle canopy patterns for every hidden triangle — small ones AND the bigger combined ones!

realLifeProject: Draw a square with both diagonals on paper, count the triangles yourself before checking the answer (8), then try a pentagon with diagonals from one corner and verify the n−2 formula.

rememberIt.unpack: Total shapes = smallest regions + every valid combination of adjacent regions.

studentQuestions.q: Is there a shortcut for counting squares or other shapes too, not just triangles?
studentQuestions.a: Not one universal formula like n−2, but the same 'small regions first, then check combinations' method works for any shape — squares, rectangles, or any polygon you're asked to count.

studentQuestions.q: What if the figure is too complex to count by eye?
studentQuestions.a: Label every smallest region with a number or letter, then systematically list which labels combine to form each valid shape — this turns a visual guessing game into a reliable, checkable list.
